key_insight: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are a powerful basis for human uplift studies of frontier AI, but they must be adapted to account for AI-specific threats (adaptivity, interference, nonstationarity, heterogeneous effects). The paper gives concrete design and analysis adjustments to make uplift estimates reliable for high-stakes decisions.
problem_solved: Addresses the gap between standard RCT methodology and the distinctive properties of frontier AI systems that can bias or invalidate human uplift estimates—helping practitioners avoid misleading conclusions when using RCTs to inform deployment, governance, and safety choices.
method: Systematically diagnose AI-specific threats to causal inference (model adaptivity, user/agent interference, distributional drift, measurement and anchoring biases).
Prescribe tailored design fixes: blocking and stratified randomization, staggered/clustered rollouts, repeated-measures and A/A checks, adaptive sample sizing and pre-registration.
Provide analysis and robustness toolset: heterogeneity analysis, sensitivity analyses and bounds, external-validity checks, and predefined operational stopping/safety rules.
impact: Gives AI/ML teams and decision-makers practical protocols to run credible human uplift RCTs for frontier models, improving the reliability of evaluation results and reducing the chance of harmful deployment decisions in safety-critical contexts.

paper_title: RCTs & Human Uplift Studies: Methodological Challenges and Practical Solutions for Frontier AI Evaluation
paper_authors: Patricia Paskov, Kevin Wei, Shen Zhou Hong, Dan Bateyko, Xavier Roberts-Gaal
